newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Jackson provokes unholy scenes in Prague cathedral.
newsitem.headline: Jackson provokes unholy scenes in Prague cathedral.

text.p: Michael Jackson, the self-styled King of Pop, provoked some unholy behaviour in Prague's St Vitus cathedral on Friday before dropping in on President Vaclav Havel, a self-confessed Rolling Stones fanatic.

The U.S. megastar, who picked Prague to launch his first concert tour in more than two years, startled tourists enjoying St Vitus's gothic splendour when he made a surprise visit to the cathedral packed with sightseers.
Visitors gaped or clamboured onto pews to get a better view of Jackson, dressed in a black jacket with military-style epaulettes and his trademark black wide-rimmed hat.
Some disturbed the solemn peace of one of Europe's great sacred buildings, chanting "Michael, Michael".
Jackson, who is scheduled to perform on Saturday night, has spent most of the time since arriving on Tuesday cloistered away in Prague's Inter-Continental Hotel.

Hundreds of fans, some near hysteria, have besieged the building, screaming and chanting appeals for their hero to show himself. They broke through a security cordon and blocked Jackson's car when he attempted a shopping trip on Thursday.

During his whirlwind cathedral tour, Jackson removed the black silk-like mask he has worn in public throughout his Prague stay as he visited the chapel of St Wenceslas, built above the tomb of Good King Wenceslas of Christmas carol fame.

Jackson then visited President Vaclav Havel in his nearby offices in the Prague castle complex, and invited him to the open-air concert to be held on a field where the Communists once staged their regimented Mayday march-pasts, a presidential statement said.
It did not say whether Havel would accept.
Havel, 59, is better known for his love of the British rock band the Rolling Stones, and rarely misses a chance to meet lead singer Mick Jagger and guitarist Keith Richards.

But Havel did not miss the Jackson phenomenon despite spending much of the 1980s in communist jails as a dissident playwright. One of Havel's essays written in prison is named after Jackson's album "Thriller".
